 1   Q:   Please state your name and business address.

 2   A:   My name is John J. Spanos. My business address is 300 Sterling Parkway, Suite

 8   A:   I am testifying on behalf of Evergy Metro, Inc. d/b/a Evergy Missouri Metro

 9        (“Evergy Missouri Metro”).

10   Q.   Please state your educational background.

11   A.   I have Bachelor of Science degrees in Industrial Management and Mathematics

12        from Carnegie-Mellon University and a Master of Business Administration from

13        York College of Pennsylvania.

14   Q.   Do you belong to any professional societies?

15   A.   Yes.   I am a past President and member of the Society of Depreciation

16        Professionals. I am also a member of the American Gas Association/Edison

17        Electric Institute Industry Accounting Committee.

  1   Q.   Do you hold any special certification as a depreciation expert?

 2   A.   Yes. The Society of Depreciation Professionals has established national standards

 3        for depreciation professionals. The Society administers an examination to become

 4        certified in this field. I passed the certification exam in September 1997, and was

 5        recertified in August 2003, February 2008, January 2013, February 2018 and

 6        February 2023.

 7   Q:   What are your responsibilities?

 8   A:   My responsibilities include conducting depreciation, valuation and original cost

 9        studies, determining service life and net salvage estimates, conducting field

10        reviews, presenting recommended depreciation rates to clients, and supporting such

11        rates before state and federal regulatory agencies.

12   Q:   Please state your qualifications.

13   A:   I have over 39 years of depreciation experience which includes giving expert

14        testimony in more than 520 cases before 47 regulatory commissions, including this

15        Commission. These cases have included depreciation studies in the electric, gas,

16        water, wastewater and pipeline industries. In addition to cases where I have

17        submitted testimony, I have also supervised over 900 other depreciation or

18        valuation assignments.    Please refer to Schedule JJS-2 for my qualifications

19        statement, which includes further information with respect to my work history, case

20        experience, and leadership in the Society of Depreciation Professionals.




                                                                                           2
  1   Q:   Have you previously testified in a proceeding at the Missouri Public Service

 2        Commission (“PSC” or “Commission”) or before any other utility regulatory

 3        agency?

 4   A:   Yes.

 5   Q.   What is the purpose of your testimony in this proceeding?

 6   A.   My testimony will support and explain the depreciation study conducted under my

 7        direction and supervision for the electric utility plant of Evergy Missouri Metro.

 8        The study represents all electric plant assets.

 9   Q.   Please define the concept of depreciation.

10   A.   Depreciation refers to the loss in service value not restored by current maintenance,

11        incurred in connection with the consumption or prospective retirement of utility

12        plant during service from causes which are known to be in current operation,

13        against which the Company is not protected by insurance. Among the causes to be

14        given consideration are wear and tear, decay, action of the elements, obsolescence,

15        changes in the art, changes in demand and the requirements of public authorities.

16   Q.   Have you filed any exhibits with your testimony?

17   A.   Yes. Attached to my testimony is Schedule JJS-1.

18   Q.   Was schedule JJS-1 prepared under your direction and control?

19   A.   Yes.

20   Q.   Please describe schedule JJS-1.

21   A.   Schedule JJS-1 is a report entitled, “2025 Depreciation Study - Calculated Annual

22        Depreciation Accruals Related to Electric Plant as of June 30, 2025.” This report

23        sets forth the results of my depreciation study for Evergy Missouri Metro.



                                                                                              3
  1   Q.   Is schedule JJS-1 a true and accurate copy of your depreciation study?

 2   A.   Yes.

 3   Q.   Does schedule JJS-1 accurately portray the results of your depreciation study

 4        as of June 30, 2025?

 5   A.   Yes.

 6   Q.   What was the purpose of your depreciation study?

 7   A.   The purpose of the depreciation study was to estimate the annual depreciation

 8        accruals related to electric plant in service for ratemaking purposes and determine

 9        appropriate average service lives and net salvage percentages for each plant

10        account.

11   Q.   Please describe the contents of your report.

12   A.   The Depreciation Study is presented in nine parts. Part I, Introduction, presents the

13        scope and basis for the Depreciation Study. Part II, Estimation of Survivor Curves,

14        includes descriptions of the methodology of estimating survivor curves. Parts III

15        and IV set forth the analysis for determining service life and net salvage estimates.

16        Part V, Calculation of Annual and Accrued Depreciation, includes the concepts of

17        depreciation and amortization using the remaining life basis. Part VI, Results of

18        Study, presents a description of the results of my analysis and a summary of the

19        depreciation calculations. Parts VII, VIII and IX include graphs and tables that

20        relate to the service life and net salvage analyses, and the detailed depreciation

21        calculations by account.

22               The Depreciation Study also includes several tables and tabulations of data

23        and calculations. Table 1 on pages VI-4 through VI-9 of the Depreciation Study



                                                                                             4
  1        presents the estimated survivor curve, the net salvage percent, the original cost as

 2        of June 30, 2025, the book depreciation reserve, and the calculated annual

 3        depreciation accrual and rate for each account or subaccount.            The section

 4        beginning on page VII-2 presents the results of the retirement rate analyses

 5        prepared as the historical bases for the service life estimates. The section beginning

 6        on page VIII-2 presents the results of the net salvage analysis. The section

 7        beginning on page IX-2 presents the depreciation calculations related to surviving

 8        original cost as of June 30, 2025.

 9   Q.   Please explain how you performed your depreciation study.

10   A.   I used the straight-line remaining life method of depreciation, with the average

11        service life procedure for all plant assets except some general plant accounts. The

12        annual depreciation is based on a method of depreciation accounting that seeks to

13        distribute the unrecovered cost of fixed capital assets over the estimated remaining

14        useful life of each unit, or group of assets, in a systematic and rational manner.

15               For General Plant Accounts 391.00, 391.01, 393.00, 394.00, 395.00,

16        397.010, 397.030, and 398.00, I used the straight-line remaining life method of

17        amortization. Annual amortization accounting will also apply to the related FERC

18        Order 898 accounts that were part of the asset transition in 2025. The annual

19        amortization is based on amortization accounting that distributes the unrecovered

20        cost of fixed capital assets over the remaining amortization period selected for each

21        account and vintage.




                                                                                               5
  1   Q.   How did you determine the recommended annual depreciation accrual rates?

 2   A.   I did this in two phases. In the first phase, I estimated the service life and net salvage

 3        characteristics for each depreciable group, that is, each plant account or subaccount

 4        identified as having similar characteristics. In the second phase, I calculated the

 5        composite remaining lives and annual depreciation accrual rates based on the

 6        service life and net salvage estimates determined in the first phase.

 7   Q.   Please describe the first phase of the depreciation study, in which you

 8        estimated the service life and net salvage characteristics for each depreciable

 9        group.

10   A.   The service life and net salvage study consisted of compiling historic data from

11        records related to Every Missouri Metro’s plant; analyzing these data to obtain

12        historic trends of survivor and net salvage characteristics; obtaining supplementary

13        information from Evergy Missouri Metro’s management, and operating personnel

14        concerning practices and plans as they relate to plant operations; and interpreting

15        the above data and the estimates used by other electric utilities to form judgments

16        regarding average service life and net salvage characteristics.

17   Q.   What historic data did you analyze for the purpose of estimating service life

18        characteristics?

19   A.   I analyzed the Company’s accounting entries that record plant transactions during

20        the period 1920 through 2024. The transactions included additions, retirements,

21        transfers and the related balances. The Company records also included surviving

22        dollar value by year installed for each plant account as of June 30, 2025.




                                                                                                  6
  1   Q.   What method did you use to analyze this service life data?

 2   A.   I used the retirement rate method. This is the most appropriate method when aged

 3        retirement data are available, because this method determines the average rates of

 4        retirement actually experienced by the Company during the period of time covered

 5        by the study.

 6   Q.   Please describe how you used the retirement rate method to analyze Evergy

 7        Missouri Metro’s service life data.

 8   A.   I applied the retirement rate method to each different group of property in the study.

 9        For each property group, I used the retirement rate method to form a life table

10        which, when plotted, shows an original survivor curve for that property group.

11        Each original survivor curve represents the average survivor pattern experienced

12        by the several vintage groups during the experience band studied. The survivor

13        patterns do not necessarily describe the life characteristics of the property group;

14        therefore, interpretation of the original survivor curves is required to use them as

15        valid considerations in estimating service life. The Iowa-type survivor curves were

16        used to perform these interpretations.

17   Q.   What is an “Iowa-type survivor curve” and how did you use such curves to

18        estimate the service life characteristics for each property group?

19   A.   Iowa type curves are a widely used group of generalized survivor curves that

20        contain the range of survivor characteristics usually experienced by utilities and

21        other industrial companies. The Iowa curves were developed at the Iowa State

22        College Engineering Experiment Station through an extensive process of observing




                                                                                              7
  1        and classifying the ages at which various types of property used by utilities and

 2        other industrial companies had been retired.

 3                Iowa type curves are used to smooth and extrapolate original survivor

 4        curves determined by the retirement rate method. The Iowa curves and truncated

 5        Iowa curves were used in this study to describe the forecasted rates of retirement

 6        based on the observed rates of retirement and the outlook for future retirements.

 7                The estimated survivor curve designations for each depreciable property

 8        group indicate the average service life, the family within the Iowa system to which

 9        the property group belongs, and the relative height of the mode. For example, the

10        Iowa 53-R1.5 indicates an average service life of fifty-three years; a right-moded,

11        or R, type curve (the mode occurs after average life for right-moded curves); and a

12        moderate height, 1.5, for the mode (possible modes for R type curves range from

13        0.5 to 5).

14   Q.   What approach did you use to estimate the lives of significant production

15        facilities?

16   A.   I used the life span technique to estimate the lives of significant facilities for which

17        concurrent retirement of the entire facility is anticipated. In this technique, the

18        survivor characteristics of such facilities are described using interim survivor

19        curves and estimated probable retirement dates.          The interim survivor curve

20        describes the rate of retirement related to the replacement of elements of the facility,

21        such as, for a power plant, the retirement of assets such as pumps, motors and piping

22        that occur during the life of the facility. The probable retirement date provides the

23        rate of final retirement for each year of installation for the facility by truncating the



                                                                                                 8
  1        interim survivor curve for each installation year at its attained age at the date of

 2        probable retirement. The use of interim survivor curves truncated at the date of

 3        probable retirement provides a consistent method for estimating the lives of the

 4        several years of installation for a particular facility inasmuch as a single concurrent

 5        retirement for all years of installation will occur when it is retired.

 6   Q.   Is this approach widely accepted for estimating the service lives of production

 7        facilities?

 8   A.   Yes. The life span has been used previously for Evergy Missouri Metro as well as

 9        for Evergy Missouri West. My firm has also used the life span technique in

10        performing depreciation studies presented to and accepted by many public utility

11        commissions across the United States and Canada, including Missouri.

12   Q.   What is the basis for the probable retirement year that you have estimated for

13        each facility?

14   A.   The basis for the probable retirement years are life spans for each facility that are

15        based on judgment and incorporate consideration of the age, use, size, nature of

16        construction, management outlook and typical life spans experienced and used by

17        other electric utilities for similar facilities. Most of the life spans result in probable

18        retirement years that are many years in the future. As a result, the retirements of

19        these facilities are not yet subject to specific management plans. Such plans would

20        be premature. At the appropriate time, detailed studies of the economics of

21        rehabilitation and continued use or retirement of the structure will be performed,

22        and the results incorporated in the estimation of the facility’s life span.




                                                                                                  9
  1   Q.   Are the factors considered in your estimates of service life and net salvage

 2        percents presented in schedule JJS-1?

 3   A.   Yes. A discussion of the factors considered in the estimation of service lives and

 4        net salvage percents are presented in Part III and Part IV of Schedule JJS-1.

 5   Q.   Did you physically observe Evergy Missouri Metro’s plant and equipment as

 6        part of your depreciation study?

 7   A.   Yes. There were field reviews of Evergy Missouri Metro’s property during October

 8        2025 to observe representative portions of plant. Also, I have conducted field visits

 9        in prior studies in September 2021, August 2014 and August 2009. Field reviews

10        are conducted to become familiar with Company operations and obtain an

11        understanding of the function of the plant and information with respect to the

12        reasons for past retirements and the expected future causes of retirements. This

13        knowledge was incorporated in the interpretation and extrapolation of the statistical

14        analyses.

15   Q.   How did your experience in development of other depreciation studies affect

16        your work in this case?

17   A.   Because I customarily conduct field reviews for my depreciation studies, I have had

18        the opportunity to visit scores of similar plants and meet with operations personnel

19        at other companies. The knowledge accumulated from those visits and meetings

20        provide me useful information that I can draw on to confirm or challenge my

21        numerical analyses concerning plant condition and remaining life estimates.




                                                                                            10
  1   Q.   Would you please explain the concept of “net salvage”?

 2   A.   Net salvage is a component of the service value of capital assets that is recovered

 3        through depreciation rates. The service value of an asset is its original cost less its

 4        net salvage. Net salvage is the salvage value received for the asset upon retirement

 5        less the cost to retire the asset. When the cost to retire exceeds the salvage value,

 6        the result is negative net salvage.

 7                 Inasmuch as depreciation expense is the loss in service value of an asset

 8        during a defined period, e.g. one year, it must include a ratable portion of both the

 9        original cost and the net salvage. That is, the net salvage related to an asset should

10        be incorporated in the cost of service during the same period as its original cost so

11        that customers receiving service from the asset pay rates that include a portion of

12        both elements of the asset’s service value, the original cost and the net salvage

13        value.

14                 For example, the full recovery of the service value of a $4,000 line

15        transformer will include not only the $4,000 of original cost, but also, on average,

16        $450 to remove the line transformer at the end of its life and $50 in salvage value.

17        In this example, the net salvage component is negative $400 ($50 - $450), and the

18        net salvage percent is negative 10% (($50 - $450)/$4,000).

19   Q.   Please describe how you estimated net salvage percentages.

20   A.   I estimated the net salvage percentages based on informed judgment that, for most

21        accounts, incorporated analyses of the historical data for the period 1976 through

22        2024 and considered estimates for other electric companies, experience of industry

23        practices as well as trends in the industry. In the historical analyses, the net salvage,



                                                                                                11
  1        cost of removal and gross salvage amounts were expressed as percents of the

 2        original cost retired. These percents were calculated on annual and three-year

 3        moving average bases for the 1976 to 2024 period.

 4   Q.   Were the net salvage percentages for generating facilities based on the same

 5        analyses?

 6   A.   Yes, for interim analyses. The net salvage percentages for generating facilities

 7        were based on two components, the interim net salvage percentage and the final net

 8        salvage percentage. The interim net salvage percentage is determined based on the

 9        historical indications from the period 1976-2024 for steam; 1987-2024 for nuclear;

10        1982-2024 for other production and 2010-2024 for wind. The cost of removal and

11        gross salvage amounts are based as a percentage of the associated plant retired. The

12        final net salvage or dismantlement component was determined based on the assets

13        anticipated to be retired at the concurrent date of final retirement.              The

14        decommissioning costs were determined by the 1898 & Co. study for steam, other

15        production and wind.

16               The final net salvage or decommissioning component was determined based

17        on the retirement activities associated with the assets anticipated to be retired at the

18        concurrent date of final retirement.

19   Q.   Have you included a dismantlement or decommissioning component into the

20        overall recovery of generating facilities?

21   A.   Yes. A partial dismantlement or decommissioning component has been included

22        to the net salvage percentage for steam and other production facilities including

23        wind and solar. 1898 & Co has prepared a decommissioning study and the costs



                                                                                               12
  1        utilized in the depreciation study are based on a recovery in place costs not the full

 2        dismantlement. An updated amount of decommissioning costs to retire the plants

 3        in place is currently being completed to validate the estimate provided in the Direct

 4        Filing and will update the previous estimate if necessary. Once completed, the

 5        updated estimate will be incorporated into the Depreciation Study and updated, if

 6        necessary.

 7   Q.   Can you explain how the final net salvage component is included in the

 8        depreciation study?

 9   A.   Yes. The dismantlement component is part of the overall net salvage for each

10        location within the production assets. Based on studies for other utilities and the

11        cost estimates of Evergy Missouri Metro, it was determined that the dismantlement

12        or decommissioning costs for steam, solar, wind and other production facilities is

13        best calculated by dividing the dismantlement cost by the surviving plant at final

14        retirement. These amounts on a location basis are added to the interim net salvage

15        percentage of the assets anticipated to be retired on an interim basis to produce the

16        weighted net salvage percentage for each location. The detailed calculations of the

17        overall net salvage for each location is set forth on pages VIII-2 and VIII-3 of

18        Schedule JJS-1.

19   Q.   What is the basis of the dismantlement or decommissioning cost estimates?

20   A.   The decommissioning cost estimates are based on decommissioning studies of each

21        generating site performed by 1898 & Co. These estimates are based on costs to

22        partially dismantle the facilities. The amount included as terminal net salvage is

23        based on the costs to retire the assets of the facilities in place, and not to physically



                                                                                                13
  1        remove/decommission all assets at each location.            Although, the costs to

 2        decommission power plants has tended to increase over time (as have construction

 3        costs in general) there is no escalation of the costs to the time of retirement.

 4   Q.   Please describe the second phase of the process that you used in the

 5        depreciation study in which you calculated composite remaining lives and

 6        annual depreciation accrual rates.

 7   A.   After I estimated the service life and net salvage characteristics for each depreciable

 8        property group, I calculated the annual depreciation accrual rates for each

 9        depreciable group based on the straight-line remaining life method, using

10        remaining lives weighted consistent with the average service life procedure. The

11        calculation of annual depreciation accrual rates was developed as of June 30, 2025.

12   Q.   Please describe the straight-line remaining life method of depreciation.

13   A.   The straight-line remaining life method of depreciation allocates the original cost

14        of the property, less accumulated depreciation, less future net salvage, in equal

15        amounts to each year of remaining service life.

16   Q.   Please describe the average service life procedure for calculating remaining

17        life accrual rates.

18   A.   The average service life procedure defines the group for which the remaining life

19        annual accrual is determined. Under this procedure, the annual accrual rate is

20        determined for the entire group or account based on its average remaining life and

21        this rate is applied to the surviving balance of the group’s cost. The average

22        remaining life of the group is calculated by first dividing the future book accruals

23        (original cost less allocated book reserve less future net salvage) by the average



                                                                                              14
  1        remaining life for each vintage. The average remaining life for each vintage is

 2        derived from the area under the survivor curve between the attained age of the

 3        vintage and the maximum age. Then, the sum of the future book accruals is divided

 4        by the sum of the annual accruals to determine the average remaining life of the

 5        entire group for use in calculating the annual depreciation accrual rate.

 6   Q.   Please describe amortization accounting.

 7   A.   Amortization accounting is used for accounts with many units, but small asset

 8        values. In amortization accounting, units of property are capitalized in the same

 9        manner as they are in depreciation accounting. However, depreciation accounting

10        is difficult for these assets because periodic inventories are required to properly

11        reflect plant in service. Consequently, retirements are recorded when a vintage is

12        fully amortized rather than as the units are removed from service. That is, there is

13        no dispersion of retirement. All units are retired when the age of the vintage reaches

14        the amortization period. Each plant account or group of assets is assigned a fixed

15        period which represents an anticipated life during which the asset will render

16        service. For example, in amortization accounting, assets that have a 20-year

17        amortization period will be fully recovered after 20 years of service and taken off

18        the Company books but not necessarily removed from service. In contrast, assets

19        that are taken out of service before 20 years remain on the books until the

20        amortization period for that vintage has expired.

21   Q.   Amortization accounting is being utilized for which plant accounts?

22   A.   Amortization accounting is only appropriate for certain General Plant accounts.

23        These accounts are 391.00, 391.01, 393.00, 394.00, 395.00, 397.010, 397.030, and



                                                                                             15
  1        398.00, which represent about three percent of depreciable plant. Amortization

 2        accounting will also apply to the related FERC Order 898 accounts that were part

 3        of the asset transition in 2025.

 4   Q.   Does complete implementation of amortization accounting include a reserve

 5        amortization?

 6   A.   Yes. In order to achieve the proper amortization rate for each account, the book

 7        reserve must be aligned to surviving vintages in a manner that assigns the

 8        appropriate reserve to each vintage within each account. The required book reserve

 9        for each account will need to be segregated from the current levels in order to

10        achieve the appropriate amortization rate.      The excess or deficiency will be

11        amortized over a 5-year period. This will allow current and future assets to be

12        recovered consistently with the amortization period and accounting of the assets by

13        account. The reserve adjustment for amortization is set forth in on page VI-9 of

14        Schedule JJS-1.

15   Q.   Please use an example to illustrate the development of the annual depreciation

16        accrual rate for a particular group of property in your depreciation study.

17   A.   I will use Account 367, Underground Conductors and Devices, as an example

18        because it is one of the largest depreciable groups.

19               The retirement rate method was used to analyze the survivor characteristics

20        of this property group. Aged plant accounting data were compiled from 1947

21        through 2024 and analyzed in periods that best represent the overall service life of

22        this property. The life tables for the 1947-2024 and 1985-2024 experience bands

23        are presented in the depreciation study on pages VII-130 through VII-135. Each



                                                                                           16
  1   life table displays the retirement and surviving ratios of the aged plant data exposed

 2   to retirement by age interval. For example, page VII-130 of Schedule JJS-1, shows

 3   $2,284,075 retired during age interval 0.5-1.5 with $877,115,272 exposed to

 4   retirement at the beginning of the interval. Consequently, the retirement ratio is

 5   0.0026 ($2,284,075/$877,115,272) and the survivor ratio is 0.9974(1-0.0026). The

 6   percent surviving at age 0.5 of .9987 percent is multiplied by the survivor ratio of

 7   99.74 to derive the percent surviving at age 1.5 of 99.61 percent. This process

 8   continues for the remaining age intervals for which plant was exposed to retirement

 9   during the period 1947-2024. The life tables, or original survivor curves, are plotted

10   along with the estimated smooth survivor curve, the 57-R1.5, on page VII-129 of

11   Schedule JJS-1.

12           The net salvage percent is presented on pages VIII-74 through VIII-76 of

13   Schedule JJS-1. The percentage is based on the result of annual gross salvage

14   minus the cost to remove plant assets as compared to the original cost of plant

15   retired during the period 1976 through 2024. The 49-year period experienced

16   negative $18,834,680 ($22,083,256-$40,917,935) in net salvage for $71,034,377

17   plant   retired.   The   result   is   negative   net   salvage    of   27    percent

18   ($18,834,680/$71,034,377); however, the most recent five-year period and the

19   rolling three-year averages trend toward negative 75 and negative 86 percent,

20   respectively. Therefore, based on the overall statistics, company expectations for

21   the future and industry averages, negative twenty-five percent was recommended.

22           My calculation of the annual depreciation related to original cost of electric

23   utility plant as of June 30, 2025, for Account 367 is presented on pages IX-146 and



                                                                                        17
  1        IX-147 of Schedule JJS-1. The calculation is based on the 57-R1.5 survivor curve,

 2        25% negative net salvage, the attained age, and the allocated book reserve. The

 3        tabulation sets forth the installation year, the original cost, calculated accrued

 4        depreciation, allocated book reserve, future accruals, remaining life and annual

 5        accrual. These totals are brought forward to Table 1 on page VI-8.

 6   Q.   In your opinion, are the depreciation and amortization rates set forth in

 7        Schedule JJS-1 the appropriate rates for the commission to adopt in this

 8        proceeding for Evergy Missouri Metro?

 9   A.   Yes. These rates appropriately reflect the rates at which the costs of Evergy

10        Missouri Metro’s assets are being consumed over their useful lives. These rates are

11        an appropriate basis for setting electric rates in this matter and for the Company to

12        use for booking depreciation and amortization expense going forward.

13   Q.   Have you developed depreciation rates for new or reclassified assets?

14   A.   Yes. This study includes the transition of many asset classes due to FERC Order

15        898. Each of the accounts is presented in Table 1, pages VI-4 through VI-9 of

16        Schedule JJS-1.

17   Q.   Does this conclude your testimony?

18   A.   Yes, it does.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

       Pursuant to Evergy Metro Inc.’s (“Company”) request, Gannett Fleming Valuation

and Rate Consultants, LLC (“Gannett Fleming”) conducted a depreciation study related

were based on attained ages and estimated average service life and forecasted net

salvage characteristics for each depreciable group of assets.

       The Company’s accounting policy has not changed since the last depreciation

study was prepared. However, there have been changes to the life spans of generating

facilities and estimates of life and net salvage.       Additionally, there has been a

reclassification of assets based on FERC Order 898.          The overall effect of these

changes has created an increase in depreciation expense as compared to the rates

approved in the last proceeding.

       Gannett Fleming recommends the calculated annual depreciation accrual rates set

forth herein apply specifically to electric plant in service as of June 30, 2025 as

summarized by Table 1 of the study. Supporting analysis and calculations are provided

within the study.

BASIS OF THE STUDY

Depreciation

       Depreciation, in public utility regulation, is the loss in service value not restored by

current maintenance, incurred in connection with the consumption or prospectiv e

retirement of utility plant in the course of service from causes which are known to be in

current operation and against which the utility is not protected by insurance. Among

causes to be given consideration are wear and tear, deterioration, action of the elements,

inadequacy, obsolescence, changes in the art, changes in demand, and the requirements

of public authorities.

       Depreciation, as used in accounting, is a method of distributing fixed capital costs,

less net salvage, over a period of time by allocating annual amounts to expense. Each

annual amount of such depreciation expense is part of that year's total cost of providing

electric utility service. Normally, the period of time over which the fixed capital cost is

allocated to the cost of service is equal to the period of time over which an item renders

service, that is, the item's service life. The most prevalent method of allocation is to

distribute an equal amount of cost to each year of service life. This method is known as

the straight line method of depreciation.

       For most accounts, the annual depreciation was calculated by the straight line

method using the average service life procedure and the remaining life basis. For certain

General Plant accounts, the annual depreciation is based on amortization accounting.

                     PART II. ESTIMATION OF SURVIVOR CURVES

       The calculation of annual depreciation based on the straight line method requires

the estimation of survivor curves and the selection of group depreciation procedures. The

estimation of survivor curves is discussed below, and the development of net salvage is

discussed in later sections of this report.


SURVIVOR CURVES

       The use of an average service life for a property group implies that the various

units in the group have different lives.      Thus, the average life may be obtained by

determining the separate lives of each of the units or by constructing a survivor curve by

plotting the number of units which survive at successive ages.

       The survivor curve graphically depicts the amount of property existing at each age

throughout the life of an original group. From the survivor curve, the average life of the

group, the remaining life expectancy, the probable life, and the frequency curve can be

calculated. In Figure 1, a typical smooth survivor curve and the derived curves are

illustrated. The average life is obtained by calculating the area under the survivor curve,

from age zero to the maximum age, and dividing this area by the ordinate at age zero.

The remaining life expectancy at any age can be calculated by obtaining the area under

the curve, from the observation age to the maximum age, and dividing this area by the

percent surviving at the observation age. For example, in Figure 1, the remaining life at

age 30 is equal to the crosshatched area under the survivor curve divided by 29.5 percent

surviving at age 30. The probable life at any age is developed by adding the age and

remaining life. If the probable life of the property is calculated for each year of age, the

probable life curve shown in the chart can be developed. The frequency curve presents

the number of units retired in each age interval. It is derived by obtaining the differences

between the amount of property surviving at the beginning and at the end of each interval.

Iowa Type Curves
       The range of survivor characteristics usually experienced by utility and industrial
properties is encompassed by a system of generalized survivor curves known as the Iowa

type curves. There are four families in the Iowa system, labeled in accordance with the
location of the modes of the retirements (or the portion of the frequency curve with the
highest level of retirements) in relationship to the average life and the relative height of

the modes. The left moded curves, presented in Figure 2, are those in which the greatest
frequency of retirement occurs to the left of, or prior to, average service life. The
symmetrical moded curves, presented in Figure 3, are those in which the greatest

frequency of retirement occurs at average service life. The right moded curves, presented
in Figure 4, are those in which the greatest frequency occurs to the right of, or after,
average service life. The origin moded curves, presented in Figure 5, are those in which

the greatest frequency of retirement occurs at the origin, or immediately after age zero.
The letter designation of each family of curves (L, S, R or O) represents the location of
the mode of the associated frequency curve with respect to the average service life. The

numbers represent the relative heights of the modes of the frequency curves within each
family. A higher number designates a higher mode curve.
       The Iowa curves were developed at the Iowa State College Engineering

Experiment Station through an extensive process of observation and classification of the
ages at which industrial property had been retired. A report of the study which resulted
in the classification of property survivor characteristics into 18 type curves, which

constitute three of the four families, was published in 1935 in the form of the Experiment
Station’s Bulletin 125.

Retirement Rate Method of Analysis
       The retirement rate method is an actuarial method of deriving survivor curves using
the average rates at which property of each age group is retired. The method relates to

property groups for which aged accounting experience is available and is the method
used to develop the original stub survivor curves in this study. The method (also known
as the annual rate method) is illustrated through the use of an example in the following

text and is also explained in several publications including "Statistical Analyses of
Industrial Property Retirements," 2 "Engineering Valuation and Depreciation," 3 and
"Depreciation Systems." 4

       The average rate of retirement used in the calculation of the percent surviving for
the survivor curve (life table) requires two sets of data: first, the property retired during a
period of observation, identified by the property's age at retirement; and second, the

property exposed to retirement at the beginning of the age intervals during the same
period. The period of observation is referred to as the experience band. The band of
years which represent the installation dates of the property exposed to retirement during

the experience band is referred to as the placement band. An example of the calculations
used in the development of a life table follows. The example includes schedules of annual
aged property transactions, a schedule of plant exposed to retirement, a life table and

illustrations of smoothing the stub survivor curve.

GROUP DEPRECIATION PROCEDURES

       A group procedure for depreciation is appropriate when considering more than a

single item of property. Normally the items within a group do not have identical service

lives, but have lives that are dispersed over a range of time. There are two primary group

procedures, namely, average service life and equal life group. In the average service life

procedure, the rate of annual depreciation is based on the average life or average

remaining life of the group, and this rate is applied to the surviving balances of the group's

cost. A characteristic of this procedure is that the cost of plant retired prior to average life

is not fully recouped at the time of retirement, whereas the cost of plant retired subsequent

to average life is more than fully recouped. Over the entire life cycle, the portion of cost

not recouped prior to average life is balanced by the cost recouped subsequent to

average life.
